subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How is ammonia manufactured by Haber's process? Explain the reactions of ammonia. a) ZnSO₄ b) CuSO₄ c) AgCl

verification.note: Unit 7 (VA Group Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.83-84, from the shaded sub-box "VA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7 ("7. VA, VIA, VIIA GROUP ELEMENTS & NOBLE GASES"); the book prints this question and a model answer on book p.84 as Long Answer Question 1. The 1+2+2+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CHECK (book p.84, LAQ 1): the three ammonia equations were atom-counted and all three balance. ZnSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Zn(OH)₂ + (NH₄)₂SO₄ (Zn 1, S 1, O 6, N 2, H 10 each side); CuSO₄ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ (Cu 1, S 1, O 4, N 4, H 12 each side); AgCl + 2NH₃ → [Ag(NH₃)₂]Cl (Ag 1, Cl 1, N 2, H 6 each side). THE BOOK CONTRADICTS ITSELF ON ONE LINE: under "Favorable conditions" it prints "1) Low temperature 450 - 500°C". 450-500 °C is not a low temperature, and the reason 450-500 °C is used is the opposite of the label — a low temperature would favour the exothermic forward reaction but make the rate far too slow, so a compromise, or optimum, temperature is used. This card writes "optimum temperature" and gives the reason. TWO SMALLER BOOK DEFECTS: the promoter molybdenum is printed as "MO" (the element symbol is Mo), and the catalyst is written over the arrow as "Fe + MO". NCERT VARIANT recorded, not followed: NCERT Class 12 describes the catalyst as iron oxide with small amounts of K₂O and Al₂O₃ as promoters, at about 200 atm and about 700 K. The Fastrack's finely divided iron with a molybdenum promoter is the older description and is the one an IPE examiner is most likely to expect, so it is written on the card with the NCERT version recorded in the why.

steps.label: The reaction and its nature
lines: Ammonia is made by the direct combination
3. Four moles of gas give two, so the volume
steps.why: Every condition used later in the process is read off these three features, so they have to be written first. Le Chatelier's principle is applied to them one at a time: reversible means an equilibrium can be shifted, exothermic determines the temperature, and a decrease in volume determines the pressure.
common_mistakes: Writing the equation with a single arrow. The reaction is reversible and needs the double arrow ⇌.
Giving ΔH as positive. The forward reaction gives out heat, so ΔH = −92 kJ/mol.
steps.memory_tip: Reversible, exothermic, volume decreases. Those three words determine every condition below.
steps.margin_note: Write the equation with ⇌ and ΔH on the same line. The three features can be a numbered list.

steps.label: Favourable conditions
lines: By Le Chatelier's principle the yield of NH₃
is increased by a low temperature and a
But at a low temperature the rate is too slow,
so an optimum temperature is used.
steps.why: The temperature is the one condition that is a compromise, and saying so is what an examiner looks for: a low temperature gives a high equilibrium yield but a very slow rate, so 450-500 °C is chosen as the best balance of the two. The book prints this line as "Low temperature 450 - 500 °C", which contradicts itself, and it is corrected here. NCERT describes the catalyst instead as iron oxide with small amounts of K₂O and Al₂O₃ as promoters, at about 200 atm and about 700 K; either description is accepted.
common_mistakes: Writing that a high temperature increases the yield. A high temperature increases the RATE but lowers the yield of an exothermic reaction.
Writing that low pressure favours ammonia. The forward reaction decreases the volume, so high pressure favours it.
steps.memory_tip: Temperature is a compromise, pressure is not. High pressure helps both yield and rate.
steps.margin_note: Four numbered conditions with values is what these two marks are given for. One mark is usually the values and one the Le Chatelier reasoning.

steps.label: The process
lines: 1. N₂ and H₂ are mixed in the volume ratio
3. It is passed into the catalyst chamber held
4. About 10 – 20% of the mixture is changed
5. The gases are cooled, and the ammonia
condenses to a liquid and is drawn off.
6. The unchanged N₂ and H₂ are returned to
steps.why: The process is the equilibrium conditions turned into a plant. The two steps that matter most are the removal of the ammonia by cooling, which takes a product out and lets more form, and the recirculation of the unchanged gases, which is why the low conversion at each pass is not a loss. Drying over quick lime, CaO, is not a stage of this plant — the ammonia leaves the cooler as a liquid. It belongs to the laboratory preparation from NH₄Cl and Ca(OH)₂, where the ammonia gas is dried over quick lime and never over concentrated H₂SO₄, CaCl₂ or P₄O₁₀, because all three react with it.
common_mistakes: Writing the ratio as 3 : 1. It is one volume of N₂ to three volumes of H₂, so 1 : 3.
Writing that the whole mixture changes to ammonia in one pass. Only about 10 – 20% is changed at each pass, and the rest is sent back to the catalyst chamber.
steps.memory_tip: Mix 1 : 3, compress, pass over hot iron, cool and condense, send the rest back.
steps.margin_note: A numbered list of six or seven steps earns these two marks. A paragraph of the same words usually earns fewer.

steps.label: With ZnSO₄
lines: a) Aqueous ammonia (NH₄OH) added to zinc
sulphate gives a white precipitate of zinc
steps.why: Here ammonia acts as a base: the hydroxide ion from NH₄OH precipitates the metal as its hydroxide. It is worth knowing that the precipitate dissolves again in excess ammonia, forming the complex [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺, so the white solid is seen only while the ammonia is not in excess.
common_mistakes: Writing ZnO as the precipitate. The precipitate is the hydroxide Zn(OH)₂, not the oxide.
Giving one NH₄OH instead of two. Zn²⁺ needs two hydroxide ions, so two NH₄OH are used.
steps.memory_tip: Zinc gives a white precipitate; the ammonia is acting as a base here, not as a ligand.
steps.margin_note: Equation plus the words "white precipitate" completes this mark. The colour is what an examiner looks for.

steps.label: With CuSO₄
lines: b) Excess ammonia added to copper sulphate
sulphate. Here NH₃ acts as a ligand.
steps.why: This part shows the other side of ammonia: it is a ligand as well as a base, and with copper the complex is what forms. The colour change from light blue to deep blue is the visible test, and naming it is usually part of the mark.
common_mistakes: Putting SO₄²⁻ inside the square bracket. Only the four ammonia ligands go inside the coordination sphere.
Writing the colour as green. The tetraammine copper(II) ion is deep blue.
steps.memory_tip: Copper gives a deep blue solution because four ammonia molecules bond to Cu²⁺ as ligands.
steps.margin_note: Equation plus "deep blue" is the marked pair. Naming the complex is a useful extra line.

steps.label: With AgCl
lines: c) White silver chloride dissolves in aqueous
This reaction is used to tell AgCl apart from
AgBr and AgI, which do not dissolve as
steps.why: Ammonia acts as a ligand again, and the visible result is a solid going into solution rather than a colour change. Two ammonia molecules are used because the coordination number of silver(I) is 2, not 4 as it is for copper(II).
common_mistakes: Using four ammonia molecules as for copper. Silver(I) has a coordination number of 2.
Writing that AgCl reacts to give AgOH. It dissolves as the complex; no hydroxide is formed.
steps.memory_tip: Copper takes four ammonias, silver takes two. The white solid disappears.
steps.margin_note: The equation is the mark. Adding that AgCl dissolves while AgI does not is worth one extra line if there is time.

insider_note: The half most often left incomplete is the second one: three short equations for ZnSO₄, CuSO₄ and AgCl carry three of the eight marks, so write them even if the process description has to be shortened. Say which role ammonia plays each time — base with zinc, ligand with copper and silver.
